subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 11 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about control systems — and the friendly way we meet them is through robots. The big idea is simple and powerful: a control system, and a robot, always works in three steps. It takes in input (it senses the world), it processes that information (its brain decides what to do), and it makes an output (it acts). We say a robot can sense, think and act. You meet sensors — special input devices that detect changes in the world, such as distance, light, motion, temperature and infrared sensors. You meet the data logger, a device left alone to sense and store data over time. You learn about output devices — screens, printers, lights, sounds and movement (a robot's motors and arm). And you learn the difference between application software (programs that do a job for you) and system software (like the operating system, that runs the machine itself), and that different files need different amounts of storage.

outcomes: These objectives come straight from the source unit. By the end, the child should be able to:
Explain that a control system works in three steps: input (sense), process (decide), output (act) — and that a robot is a control system.
Give examples of everyday control systems (rice cooker, streetlight, traffic lights, fridge) and point to their input, process and output.
Say what a sensor is, and name sensors that detect distance, light, motion, temperature and infrared.
Explain what a data logger is and how it is used.
Name output devices — screen, printer, light, sound (buzzer/speaker), and movement (motor, robotic arm).
Tell the difference between application software and system software, and say what an operating system is.
Order everyday files from the smallest to the biggest storage (text, audio, image, video).
Follow (trace) a set of commands to guide a robot on a grid, and fix a command list that has a mistake.
Before starting, it helps if the child knows that a computer follows instructions and that a program is a set of steps in order. A quick reminder is enough — do not spend a whole session revising.

concepts.title: Sense, think, act: what a control system is
concepts.explanation: A control system is a machine that works in three steps. It takes input (it senses the world), it processes the input (its brain, the processor, decides what to do), and it makes an output (it acts — it moves, lights up, or makes a sound). A robot is a control system that we build to do a job for us. The short way to remember it is sense — think — act. Act it out first — it teaches the whole idea in five happy minutes. Child A calls out what they see ( “a wall in front!” ) — that is input. Child B decides the rule ( “if there is a wall, stop and turn” ) — that is process.
concepts.example: Child C acts it out — that is output. Together, you three are a robot — you sense, you think, and you act.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name the three steps — sense (input), think (process), act (output) — and point to you in a simple machine like a rice cooker? Listen for the sense-think-act phrase.

concepts.title: Sensing the world: sensors and data loggers
concepts.explanation: The input usually comes from a sensor — a special input device that detects a change in the world and sends that information to the processor. Different sensors sense different things: distance (how close something is), light (bright or dark), motion (movement), temperature (heat and cold), and infrared (the invisible signal from a remote). A data logger contains a sensor, a processor and storage, and is left alone to gather data over time. Light sensor: cup your hands over a torch — “A streetlight senses the dark and switches itself on.” Temperature sensor: the rice cooker from the source senses the heat of the rice and turns down when it is cooked. Distance sensor: hold a hand near a wall — “A robot senses when a wall is close and stops before it bumps.” Infrared sensor: point a TV remote and press a button — “The remote sends an invisible signal the TV senses.” Motion sensor: walk towards an imaginary door — “It senses you move, and the light comes on.”
concepts.example: Find one real example of sensing the world: sensors and data loggers around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you match a sensor to a sensible job (light sensor to the streetlight, temperature sensor to the rice cooker)?

concepts.title: Acting on the world: outputs, and guiding the robot
concepts.explanation: The output takes what the processor decided and makes something happen we can see, hear or feel. Output devices include a screen (text, pictures, video), a printer, lights (a bulb or lamp), sound (a buzzer, speaker or bell) and movement (a motor turning wheels, or a robotic arm that lifts things). A robot's wheels and arm are outputs. When the processor decides to move, it sends commands to the motors — so guiding a robot across the floor is really the output stage in action. Sort outputs by the sense they use. “Which do we see?” — a screen, a printed page, a lamp. “Which do we hear?” — a buzzer, a speaker, a bell.
concepts.example: “Which move?” — a motor spinning a wheel, a robotic arm on a date farm lifting a box. Link each output back to a sensor: a smoke alarm senses smoke (input) and sounds a buzzer (output); a robot senses a wall (input) and its motors stop (output).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you trace a command list on the grid accurately, one square at a time, and land on the right square? Can you understand that the robot only follows the commands we give it? Can you name outputs and sort you by see/hear/feel?

concepts.title: The software that runs a robot
concepts.explanation: A robot or computer needs software — the programs that tell it what to do — and there are two kinds. Application software does a job for the user: a word processor, a spreadsheet, a browser, a music player, a game — and a robot's own task program. System software runs the machine itself: it manages files and memory, keeps the machine safe, decides which task runs first, and controls the input and output devices. The most important piece is the operating system, which oversees everything quietly in the background. Application software is like a cook who makes one dish — the writing dish, the game dish. System software is the kitchen manager, the operating system, who keeps the kitchen running and makes sure the taps and cookers work. You notice the cook's dish; you rarely notice the manager — but nothing works without them. the operating system. a web browser. virus protection. a music app. the program that manages the files.
concepts.example: Find one real example of the software that runs a robot around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: does a job for me. runs the machine. Can you sort common programs into application (does a job for me) and system (runs the machine), and say the operating system is system software?

concepts.title: A robot's memory: file sizes, and be a robot controller
concepts.explanation: A robot or computer stores its work as files, and different files need different amounts of storage. From smallest to biggest: a text file (a note) is tiny; an audio file (a song) is bigger; an image file (a photo) bigger still; a video file (a film) is the biggest of all. Games vary, depending on how many pictures, sounds and videos they hold. Then we bring the unit together: a robot senses (input), thinks (process), acts (output), runs on software, and stores files. Imagine packing each file into a suitcase. A text note is one folded shirt — it barely fills the case. A song needs a bigger case.
concepts.example: A photo needs more again. A film needs the biggest of all, because a video is really thousands of photos shown quickly, with sound too.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you order text, audio, image and video from smallest to biggest storage, and retell the whole sense-think-act picture with software and files added?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in the software that runs a robot, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A robot or computer needs software — the programs that tell it what to do — and there are two kinds. Application software does a job for the user: a word processor, a spreadsheet, a browser, a music player, a game — and a robot's own task program. System software runs the machine itself: it manages files and memory, keeps the machine safe, decides which task runs first, and controls the input and output devices. The most important piece is the operating system, which oversees everything quietly in the background. Application software is like a cook who makes one dish — the writing dish, the game dish. System software is the kitchen manager, the operating system, who keeps the kitchen running and makes sure the taps and cookers work. You notice the cook's dish; you rarely notice the manager — but nothing works without them. the operating system. a web browser. virus protection. a music app. the program that manages the files.

selfAssessment: I can these objectives come straight from the source unit. By the end, the child should be able to:
I can explain that a control system works in three steps: input (sense), process (decide), output (act) — and that a robot is a control system.
I can give examples of everyday control systems (rice cooker, streetlight, traffic lights, fridge) and point to their input, process and output.
I can say what a sensor is, and name sensors that detect distance, light, motion, temperature and infrared.
I can explain what a data logger is and how it is used.
I can name output devices — screen, printer, light, sound (buzzer/speaker), and movement (motor, robotic arm).
I can tell the difference between application software and system software, and say what an operating system is.
I can order everyday files from the smallest to the biggest storage (text, audio, image, video).
I can follow (trace) a set of commands to guide a robot on a grid, and fix a command list that has a mistake.

I can before starting, it helps if the child knows that a computer follows instructions and that a program is a set of steps in order. A quick reminder is enough — do not spend a whole session revising.
